1.1.name: Science Process Skills
1.1.revision: Science process skills are basic skills that help scientists carry out investigations. These include observing (using senses), classifying (grouping), measuring (using tools), predicting (guessing outcomes), and communicating (sharing findings). Mastering these skills helps you think and work like a real scientist.

questions.q: Which science process skill involves using your five senses to gather information about an object?
Ravi groups animals into those with fur and those without fur. Which science process skill is he using?
After seeing dark clouds in the sky, Ali says, 'It will rain soon.' Which skill is he using?
A student uses a ruler to find the length of a leaf. Which science process skill is being used?
Presenting your experiment results in a table or chart is an example of which science process skill?

1.2.name: Using Space-Time Relationship
1.2.revision: Space-time relationship describes how objects change position or shape over time. For example, a seed growing into a plant changes in height (space) over days (time). Understanding this helps us describe movements, growth, and changes in the world around us.

questions.q: A plant grows from 10 cm to 25 cm over 2 weeks. What does this change describe?
A car moves from Kuala Lumpur to Penang in 4 hours. What two things are being related?
Which of the following shows a space-time relationship?
A balloon deflates from 30 cm wide to 10 cm wide in 5 seconds. The change in size over time describes...
A shadow moves from the left side of a tree to the right side during the day. This change is due to...
a: The sun's position changing over time

1.3.name: Interpreting Data
1.3.revision: Interpreting data means looking at information in tables, charts, or graphs to find patterns and draw conclusions. For example, a bar chart showing rainfall each month helps us see which month is the wettest. Scientists use this skill to make sense of their results.

questions.q: A table shows that plants watered daily grow 15 cm tall, while plants watered once a week grow 5 cm tall. What can you conclude?
a: More water makes plants grow taller

questions.q: A bar chart shows temperature from Monday to Friday. Monday is 28°C, Tuesday 29°C, Wednesday 30°C, Thursday 31°C, Friday 32°C. What pattern do you see?
After interpreting data from an experiment, what should you do next?
a: Make a conclusion based on the pattern

questions.q: A pictograph shows 5 books read by Class A, 8 by Class B, and 3 by Class C. Which class read the most books?
Data shows that a rubber band stretches longer when more weight is added. This shows a pattern of...
a: The more weight, the less stretch
The more weight, the more stretch

1.4.name: Defining Operationally
1.4.revision: Defining operationally means describing a variable by how you measure it or what you do in an experiment. For example, 'growth' can be defined operationally as 'the increase in height in centimetres measured with a ruler.' This makes experiments clear and repeatable.

questions.q: In an experiment, 'plant growth' is defined as 'increase in height in cm per week.' This is called...
A student defines 'hot water' as 'water heated to 80°C.' This is an example of...
Which of the following is an operational definition of 'loud sound'?
a: Sound measured at 90 decibels using a sound meter

questions.q: Why do scientists use operational definitions in experiments?
a: So others can repeat the experiment exactly

questions.q: In an experiment on friction, 'rough surface' is defined as 'sandpaper with grade 80.' This is an example of...

1.5.name: Controlling Variables
1.5.revision: In experiments, variables are things that can change. The manipulated variable is what you change on purpose, the responding variable is what you measure, and the constant variables stay the same. Controlling variables ensures fair tests and accurate results.

questions.q: In an experiment testing how light affects plant growth, what is the manipulated variable?
In a fair test, which variables should be kept the same?
A student wants to test which type of material absorbs water best. What is the responding variable?
To test how surface affects rolling distance, you change the surface but keep the ramp height and ball the same. What is the constant variable?
a: Both B and C are wrong

questions.q: Why must you only change ONE variable at a time in an experiment?
a: To know which variable caused the result

1.6.name: Making a Hypothesis
1.6.revision: A hypothesis is an educated guess or prediction based on what you already know. It is written as an 'if... then...' statement, such as 'If a plant gets more sunlight, then it will grow taller.' A hypothesis guides the experiment and can be tested.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correctly written hypothesis?
a: If I add more salt, then the water will boil faster

questions.q: A hypothesis must be...
A student hypothesises that 'if I use a smoother surface, then the ball will roll further.' What is the manipulated variable?
What makes a hypothesis different from a simple guess?
a: It is based on prior knowledge

questions.q: After testing a hypothesis, if the results do not match your prediction, what should you do?
a: Accept that your hypothesis was wrong and learn from it

1.7.name: Experimenting
1.7.revision: Experimenting is the complete process of carrying out a scientific investigation. The steps include: identifying the problem, making a hypothesis, planning the experiment, conducting the experiment, collecting data, interpreting data, and making a conclusion. A fair test with controlled variables is essential.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step in a scientific experiment?
After conducting an experiment and collecting data, what is the next step?
A fair test means...
a: Only one variable is changed while others stay the same

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments several times?
a: To get more accurate and reliable results

questions.q: The final step in an experiment is to...
a: Write a conclusion and report your findings

2.1.name: Organs Involved in Human Breathing
2.1.revision: The human breathing system includes the nose, trachea (windpipe), bronchi, lungs, and diaphragm. Air enters through the nose, travels down the trachea into the bronchi, and reaches the lungs where oxygen is absorbed into the blood. The diaphragm is a muscle below the lungs that helps with breathing.

The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that helps with breathing is called the...
Where does the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide take place?
Which of the following is NOT part of the human breathing system?

To make the nose look bigger

2.2.name: Human Breathing Process
2.2.revision: Breathing involves two processes: inhalation (breathing in) and exhalation (breathing out). During inhalation, oxygen from the air enters the lungs and is absorbed into the blood. During exhalation, carbon dioxide is removed from the body. Oxygen is needed by cells to produce energy.

Why do we need oxygen in our body?
a: To produce energy for our cells

2.3.name: Chest Movement During Breathing
2.3.revision: During breathing, the chest moves because of the ribs and diaphragm. When we inhale, the rib cage moves up and out and the diaphragm contracts downward, making the chest cavity bigger. When we exhale, the rib cage moves down and in and the diaphragm relaxes upward, making the chest cavity smaller.

What happens to the chest cavity size during inhalation?

2.4.name: Excretion and Defecation
2.4.revision: Excretion is the removal of waste products produced by the body, such as urine (from kidneys), carbon dioxide (from lungs), and sweat (from skin). Defecation is the removal of undigested food (faeces) from the body through the anus. These processes keep the body healthy.

questions.q: Which organ is responsible for removing excess water and waste as urine?
The removal of undigested food from the body is called...
Which of the following is an excretory organ?
Carbon dioxide is removed from the body through which organ?
The main difference between excretion and defecation is that excretion removes...

2.5.name: Response to Stimuli
2.5.revision: Humans respond to stimuli through their five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), touch (skin), taste (tongue), and smell (nose). Each sense organ detects specific stimuli - light, sound, pressure, chemicals, and odours. Our body reacts automatically or deliberately to these stimuli.

When you touch a hot pan, you quickly pull your hand away. This is an example of...
The tongue can detect which of the following tastes?
The smell of durian can be detected from far away. This is because the nose detects...
If someone whispers behind you, which stimulus do your ears detect?

2.6.name: Habits that Disrupt Human Response
2.6.revision: Certain habits can damage our sense organs and disrupt our response to stimuli. Smoking damages the lungs and reduces smell and taste. Listening to loud music can damage hearing. Drugs and alcohol affect the brain and slow down responses. Protecting our senses helps us stay healthy and safe.

questions.q: Which habit can damage your hearing?
a: Listening to loud music with earphones

questions.q: Smoking can damage which sense the most?
Drinking alcohol can affect a person's ability to...
Why should you not look directly at the sun?
a: It can damage your eyes permanently

questions.q: Using drugs without a doctor's prescription can affect which part of the body the most?

3.1.name: Breathing Organs of Animals
3.1.revision: Different animals have different breathing organs. Fish breathe through gills (taking in oxygen from water). Mammals like cats and humans use lungs. Frogs use moist skin and lungs. Insects like grasshoppers use tiny tubes called spiracles. The breathing organ depends on the animal's habitat.

A grasshopper breathes through tiny holes on its body called...
Which animal uses both moist skin and lungs to breathe?
Dolphins live in water but breathe through...
A tadpole breathes through which organ before it becomes a frog?

3.2.name: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
3.2.revision: Animals can be divided into two main groups: vertebrates (animals with a backbone) and invertebrates (animals without a backbone). Vertebrates include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Invertebrates include insects, spiders, worms, jellyfish, and snails. Most animals on Earth are invertebrates.

Which of the following is an invertebrate?
Which group of animals has a backbone and gives birth to live young?

Which of the following is a vertebrate?

3.3.name: Specific Characteristics of Vertebrates
3.3.revision: Vertebrates are grouped into five classes: fish (live in water, scales, gills, lay eggs), amphibians (moist skin, live on land and water), reptiles (dry scaly skin, lay eggs), birds (feathers, wings, beak, lay eggs), and mammals (fur/hair, feed milk to young, usually give birth). Each class has unique features.

questions.q: Which class of vertebrates has feathers and lays eggs?
A crocodile has dry scaly skin and lays eggs. It belongs to which class?
Which characteristic is unique to mammals?
a: They feed their young with milk

4.1.name: Plant Responses to Stimuli
4.1.revision: Plants respond to stimuli even though they cannot move like animals. Phototropism is growth towards light. Geotropism (gravitropism) is growth in response to gravity — roots grow downward, stems grow upward. Hydrotropism is roots growing towards water. Thigmotropism is response to touch, like a mimosa plant folding its leaves.

Roots of a plant grow downwards due to gravity. This is called...
The mimosa plant (touch-me-not) folds its leaves when touched. This is an example of...
When plant roots grow towards a water source, this response is called...
What is the main reason a sunflower turns to face the sun during the day?
a: To get more light for photosynthesis

4.2.name: Photosynthesis
4.2.revision: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food. Plants need sunlight, carbon dioxide (from air), water (from soil), and chlorophyll (green pigment in leaves) to carry out photosynthesis. The products are glucose (food for the plant) and oxygen (released into the air). Photosynthesis happens in the leaves.

What is the green substance in leaves that traps sunlight for photosynthesis?
Which of the following is NOT needed for photosynthesis?
What are the products of photosynthesis?
A plant kept in a dark cupboard for a week turns yellow and weak because...
a: It did not get enough water
It could not photosynthesise without light

4.3.name: Importance of Photosynthesis
4.3.revision: Photosynthesis is vital for life on Earth. It produces food for plants and, indirectly, for animals that eat plants. It releases oxygen into the atmosphere, which animals need to breathe. Photosynthesis also helps maintain the balance of carbon dioxide and oxygen in the air, making Earth habitable for all living things.

questions.q: Why is photosynthesis important for animals?
a: Animals get oxygen and food from plants

questions.q: If all plants disappeared, what would happen to the level of oxygen in the air?
Forests are called the 'lungs of the Earth' because they...
Which of the following depends on photosynthesis for food?
a: All living things directly or indirectly

questions.q: Besides producing food, photosynthesis also helps to...
a: Reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

5.1.name: Light Travels in Straight Lines
5.1.revision: Light travels in straight lines. This property explains many everyday phenomena. For example, when you look through a straight pipe you can see the light, but not through a bent pipe. A pinhole camera works because light travels in straight lines through a tiny hole to form an upside-down image on the screen.

a: Light is blocked by the bend

5.2.name: Shadows
5.2.revision: Shadows form when light is blocked by an opaque object. The size and shape of a shadow depend on the position of the light source and the distance between the object and the screen. A shadow is largest when the object is close to the light source and smallest when the object is far from the light source.

questions.q: A shadow is formed when...
a: Light is blocked by an opaque object

questions.q: When you move a torch closer to your hand, the shadow on the wall becomes...
Why does your shadow change length during the day?
If the light source is directly above an object, the shadow will be...
A transparent object like glass will...
a: Let most light pass through, forming a faint shadow

5.3.name: Reflection of Light
5.3.revision: Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface. Smooth and shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light well, allowing us to see clear images. Rough surfaces scatter light in many directions. A periscope uses two mirrors to reflect light so you can see objects that are not directly in your line of sight.

a: Light reflects off the water surface

5.4.name: Refraction of Light
5.4.revision: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another at an angle. For example, a straw in a glass of water looks broken or bent because light travels at different speeds in air and water. Refraction makes objects underwater appear closer or larger than they really are.

Which of these is caused by refraction?
a: Seeing your face in a mirror

questions.q: When light passes from air into water, it...

5.5.name: Formation of a Rainbow
5.5.revision: A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through water droplets in the air. The water droplets act like tiny prisms that refract (bend) and disperse (spread out) white light into its seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet (ROYGBIV). Rainbows appear after rain when the sun comes out.

questions.q: What causes a rainbow to form?
a: Refraction and dispersion of light by water droplets

Which is the correct order of colours in a rainbow from the outermost to innermost?
a: Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, violet, indigo
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red
Red, yellow, orange, green, blue, violet, indigo

questions.q: When is the best time to see a rainbow?
a: After rain when the sun appears

6.1.name: Vibrations and Sound
6.1.revision: Sound is produced when objects vibrate (move back and forth quickly). For example, strumming a guitar string makes it vibrate, producing sound. When an object stops vibrating, the sound stops. The human vocal cords vibrate to produce speech. Louder sounds are produced by larger vibrations.

questions.q: Sound is produced when objects...
When you pluck a guitar string, it vibrates and produces sound. If you hold the string still, the sound...

a: Air passes through them and they vibrate

questions.q: If you hit a drum harder, the sound becomes louder because the drum skin...

6.2.name: Sound Travels
6.2.revision: Sound can travel through solids, liquids, and gases. Sound travels fastest through solids because the particles are packed closely together, allowing vibrations to pass quickly. Sound travels slower through liquids and slowest through gases (air). Sound cannot travel through a vacuum (empty space) because there are no particles to vibrate.

questions.q: Through which medium does sound travel the fastest?
Can sound travel through a vacuum (empty space)?
a: No, sound needs a medium to travel

6.3.name: Sound Can Be Reflected
6.3.revision: Sound can be reflected by hard surfaces, producing an echo. An echo is the repetition of a sound caused by the reflection of sound waves off a surface like a wall or cliff. Sonar (Sound Navigation and Ranging) uses reflected sound to detect objects underwater, such as fish or shipwrecks.

6.4.name: Useful and Harmful Sounds
6.4.revision: Sounds can be useful (music, alarms, communication) or harmful (noise pollution). Noise pollution is unwanted loud sound that can damage hearing, cause stress, and disturb sleep. Sources of noise pollution include traffic, construction, and loud machines. We can reduce noise by using earplugs, soundproofing, and keeping volumes low.

Which of the following can help reduce noise pollution?
Sound that is useful for communication includes...
Why should you wear earplugs when operating loud machinery?
a: To protect your hearing from damage

7.1.name: Energy and Their Sources
7.1.revision: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. The main source of energy on Earth is the Sun. Other energy sources include food (chemical energy), fuel (petrol, coal, natural gas), wind, water (hydroelectric), and geothermal heat. Without energy, nothing can move, grow, or change.

Which of these is a source of energy for living things?

7.2.name: Forms of Energy
7.2.revision: Energy exists in many forms: heat (thermal), light, sound, electrical, kinetic (movement), potential (stored), and chemical (stored in food and fuel). Each form of energy can be used for different purposes. For example, electrical energy powers devices, light energy helps us see, and heat energy cooks food.

7.3.name: Transformations of Energy
7.3.revision: Energy can change from one form to another. This is called energy transformation. For example, a television converts electrical energy into light and sound energy. A fan converts electrical energy into kinetic energy (movement). A plant converts light energy from the sun into chemical energy (food) through photosynthesis.

7.4.name: Renewable and Non-renewable Energy
7.4.revision: Renewable energy sources can be replenished naturally and will not run out, such as sunlight (solar), wind, water (hydro), and geothermal. Non-renewable energy sources are limited and will eventually run out, such as coal, petroleum (oil), and natural gas. These are called fossil fuels and take millions of years to form.

7.5.name: Using Energy Wisely
7.5.revision: We must use energy wisely to save resources and reduce pollution. Simple habits can help conserve energy: turning off lights and fans when not in use, using energy-efficient appliances, taking shorter showers, using public transport, and switching off electronic devices at the plug. Saving energy also saves money and protects the environment.

a: Save energy and reduce air pollution

8.1.name: Basic Sources of Materials
8.1.revision: Materials come from natural or synthetic sources. Natural materials come from plants (wood, cotton, rubber), animals (wool, silk, leather), and minerals (metal ores, clay, sand). Synthetic materials are made by humans through chemical processes, such as plastic, nylon, and glass. Understanding where materials come from helps us use them responsibly.

Glass is made by heating which natural material?

8.2.name: Properties of Materials
8.2.revision: Materials have different properties that determine how they are used. These include strength (ability to withstand force), flexibility (ability to bend without breaking), water resistance (ability to repel water), electrical conductivity (ability to conduct electricity), transparency (ability to let light through), and hardness. Each property makes a material suitable for certain uses.

8.3.name: Applications of Properties of Materials
8.3.revision: We choose materials based on their properties for specific purposes. For example, rubber is used for tyres because it is flexible and strong. Cotton is used for clothing because it is soft and absorbs sweat. Metal is used for bridges because it is strong and durable. Choosing the right material ensures safety, comfort, and effectiveness.

questions.q: Why are cooking pots usually made of metal?
Why are car tyres made of rubber?
a: Rubber is flexible and provides grip

questions.q: Why is cotton used to make T-shirts?
a: It is soft and absorbs sweat

questions.q: A telescope lens is made of glass because glass is...
a: Transparent and can be shaped into lenses

questions.q: Wood is commonly used to make furniture because it is...
a: Strong, durable, and can be shaped

9.1.name: Gravity of Earth
9.1.revision: Gravity is a force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth. It is why things fall downwards when dropped. Earth's gravity keeps us on the ground and keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth. The force of gravity depends on mass — the more mass an object has, the stronger its gravitational pull.

Which planet has the strongest gravity in our solar system?

There is no gravity in space

questions.q: Without gravity, what would happen on Earth?
A feather and a stone are dropped at the same time. In normal air, which hits the ground first?
a: They hit at the same time

9.2.name: Rotation of Earth
9.2.revision: The Earth rotates (spins) around its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. One complete rotation takes about 24 hours (one day). The Earth rotates from west to east, which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. Rotation causes day and night.

9.3.name: Effects of Rotation of Earth
9.3.revision: Earth's rotation causes several effects: day and night cycles, the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky, and the apparent movement of stars at night. Different parts of Earth face the Sun at different times, so when it is daytime in Malaysia, it is nighttime in Brazil. Rotation also causes the Coriolis effect on wind and ocean currents.

9.4.name: Revolution of Earth
9.4.revision: Revolution is the movement of Earth around the Sun in a fixed path called an orbit. One complete revolution takes about 365 days (one year). Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical (oval-shaped). The combination of Earth's revolution and its tilted axis causes the four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

a: The distance from the Sun changing greatly

questions.q: During which season are the days longest in the Northern Hemisphere?

9.5.name: The Solar System
9.5.revision: The Solar System consists of the Sun (a star) and everything that orbits it, including eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune (in order from the Sun). The Moon orbits Earth. There are also dwarf planets (like Pluto), asteroids, and comets. The Sun is the centre of the Solar System.

Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
Which planet is closest to the Sun?

Which planet is known as the 'Red Planet'?

10.1.name: Lever
10.1.revision: A lever is a simple machine consisting of a rigid bar that pivots at a fixed point called a fulcrum. The three parts of a lever are the load (object being moved), the fulcrum (pivot point), and the force (effort applied). There are three classes of levers depending on the arrangement of load, fulcrum, and force. Examples include see-saws, scissors, and wheelbarrows.

10.2.name: Simple Machines
10.2.revision: Simple machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of force. The six types of simple machines are: lever, pulley (rope over a wheel to lift objects), inclined plane (sloping surface like a ramp), wedge (two inclined planes like a knife), screw (inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder), and wheel and axle (wheel attached to a rod, like a steering wheel).

10.3.name: Complex Machines
10.3.revision: Complex machines are made by combining two or more simple machines. For example, a bicycle combines wheels and axles, levers (brakes and pedals), and pulleys (chain and gears).
